ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Cheddar Man
famous.story_individual:
Cheddar Man lived in the western reaches of the island of Great Britain, in an area known as Cheddar Gorge. He lived during the Mesolithic era, before the arrival of agriculture to the British Isles, and may have been among the earliest people to settle in Great Britain. The condition of the remains suggests that Cheddar Man died a violent death. A large crater-like lesion just above the skull's right orbit suggests he may have also been suffering from a bone infection. Genomic research suggests that he may have been lactose intolerant, have darker skin pigmentation, blue-colored eyes and black hair.

Pictured: Reconstructed head of Cheddar Man based on the shape of his skull and DNA analysis, shown at the National History Museum in London. Wx8, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Vistegutten
famous.story_individual:
Viste Boy (Norwegian: Vistegutten) is the name given to the remains of a 15-year-old boy from the Mesolithic (middle stone age) who was found in an archaeological excavation of the Viste cave in Vistehola, Rogaland, Norway in 1907. Viste Boy is the best-preserved stone age skeleton from Norway.

The boy was very short, 125 cm (4′ 1″) tall, but had a robust build. That corresponds to the average height of an 8 or 9-year-old in the present day, even though his remains suggest he was around 15 years old at the time of death. His skull had an anomaly called Scaphocephaly, caused by premature closure of the sagittal suture, which forces the skull to grow forwards and backward but not sideways. With his short stature and different head shape, he would have had a unique appearance in his hunter-gatherer community.

Sculptor and archaeologist Oscar D. Nilsson reconstructed the boy based on the skeleton, and the model is on display at the archaeological exhibition at Hå Gamle Prestegard, Norway. Nilsson notes that the brown eyes, the intermediate skin tone, and the dark brown hair is based on other findings from the same region and time. His own DNA was not well preserved enough to tell about his colors. The skeleton’s carbon-13 stable isotope values indicate that his diet contained a lot of seafood, matching the fishing equipment in Nilsson’s model.

Viste Boy’s DNA has been sequenced, but the DNA test results have not yet been published. The haplogroup information comes from a presentation by Sean Denham at the Museum of Archaeology, University of Stavanger on February 26, 2019. His mtDNA haplogroup was U5a2b, common among hunter-gatherers.

Archaeological and genetic information sourced from Wikipedia. Reconstruction photos provided by O D Nilsson.

Technical note: Wikipedia cites the Denham 2019 presentation and states that Vistegutten’s Y-DNA haplogroup was I2a1b, most common in the western Balkans, without clarifying which ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree version that is referenced. ISOGG 2017 I2a1b-M423 best fits this description, but ISOGG 2019 I2a1b-P214 is another option. The haplogroup may be updated in the future to reflect any clarifications.

famous.name: Motala Woman
famous.story_individual:
Motala Woman (“Motala 1”) was discovered in a Mesolithic settlement and ritual complex in the town of Motala, near lake Vättern in Sweden. She lived approximately 7,600 years ago during the Upper Paleolithic. Based on her remains and the age of the site, she was thought to have been a hunter-gatherer living in the pristine, yet temperate regions of central Scandinavia.

Reconstruction of the Motala 1 woman by Oscar Nilsson

Sculptor and archaeologist Oscar D. Nilsson in collaboration with National Geographic reconstructed the face of the woman based on the skull and chose to dress her with a badger on her head, one of the animal species also found together with the human remains. The model is on display at the Motala Museum in the Charlottenborg manor house.

Reconstruction of the Kanalfjorden site with the skulls placed on poles, on display at the Motala Museum, Charlottenborg. Photo: Göran Runfeldt

Motala 1 reconstruction photos provided by O D Nilsson.

famous.name: Lola
famous.story_individual:
A single piece of chewed birch tar, discarded nearly 5,700 years ago in what is now southern Denmark, has revealed detailed information about a young woman whom scientists call "Lola." This remarkable preservation of her DNA in ancient "chewing gum" has provided one of our most complete windows into life during the transition between the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods in Scandinavia.

Genetic analysis indicates she likely had dark skin, dark brown hair, and blue eyes. Her DNA shows she was closely related to Western Hunter-Gatherers from mainland Europe, rather than those from central Scandinavia. Despite living at the beginning of the Neolithic period, when farming was spreading across Europe, she had no detectable ancestry from farming communities.

The archaeological site where the birch tar was found, Syltholm, was a coastal area near a brackish lagoon protected by sand barriers. The location contains evidence of long-term human activity, with remains of wooden fish traps and bones from various animals including cattle, deer, ox, wildcats, dogs, and otters.

The birch tar preserved not only her DNA but also traces of her diet. Genetic material from mallard duck and hazelnuts suggests these were among her recent meals. Her oral microbiome was also preserved, showing the presence of several bacteria associated with periodontal disease and the Epstein-Barr virus, though the presence of these microorganisms doesn't necessarily indicate illness.

This discovery has important implications for our understanding of the Neolithic transition in southern Scandinavia. The evidence suggests that hunter-gatherer communities maintained their traditional lifestyles even as farming began to spread through Europe. Additionally, the preservation of DNA in birch tar opens new possibilities for studying ancient populations in locations where no skeletal remains have been found.

References

  • Jensen, T. Z., Niemann, J., Iversen, K. H., Fotakis, A. K., Gopalakrishnan, S., Vågene, Å. J., Pedersen, M. W., Sinding, M., Ellegaard, M. R., Allentoft, M. E., Lanigan, L. T., Taurozzi, A. J., Nielsen, S. H., Dee, M. W., Mortensen, M. N., Christensen, M. C., Sørensen, S. A., Collins, M. J., Gilbert, M. T., . . . Schroeder, H. (2019). A 5700 year-old human genome and oral microbiome from chewed birch pitch. Nature Communications, 10(1), 1-10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-13549-9

  • The Guardian: Neolithic chewing gum helps recreate image of ancient Dane

Pictured: The piece of birch tar found in Syltholm. Jensen et al. 2019, CC-BY 4.0.

famous.name: Ötzi the Iceman
famous.story_individual:
Ötzi is one of the world’s most famous natural mummies, as his body is well-preserved and very well studied. Ötzi was about 45 years old at the time of death and enjoyed a last meal of possible ibex and wheat among other crops, some of which remained undigested in his body. Although genetically he is affiliated with hunter-gathering groups, his diet shows domesticated plants suggesting he had access to agricultural foods too.

His body was found thawing in the Italian Alps where some archaeologists hypothesize that he may have been murdered, as a spearhead was found lodged in his shoulder.

He lived 5300 years ago during the Chalcolithic period, which is also referred to as the Copper Age (before the Bronze Age).

Forensic/artistic reconstruction of Ötzi. © South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology/Augustin Ochsenreiter

famous.name: Thuya
famous.story_individual:
Thuya was a prominent noblewoman in the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. She held several prestigious titles including "Singer of Hathor" and "Chief of the Entertainers," indicating her significant role in religious and court life.

She married Yuya, a powerful adviser to Pharaoh Amenhotep III, and together they became one of the most influential couples of their time. Their daughter Tiye went on to become the Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III, elevating the family's status even further. Through Tiye, Thuya became the great-grandmother of the famous pharaoh Tutankhamun.

Thuya was buried alongside her husband Yuya in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes. Their tomb (KV46) was discovered in 1905 and was remarkably well-preserved, being one of the few non-royal tombs in the valley. The mummies of both Thuya and Yuya were found in excellent condition, allowing for later DNA analysis.

Modern genetic studies, including those conducted by Zahi Hawass et al. in 2010, confirmed Thuya's biological relationship to several members of the royal family. The DNA analysis proved that she was indeed the grandmother of both Akhenaten and The Younger Lady (KV35YL), who were the parents of Tutankhamun.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

The same studies revealed that Thuya lived to be around 50-60 years old, based on examination of her mummy. Her preserved remains show she had long, wavy white hair, and she appears to have been treated with the highest respect in death, as evidenced by the quality of her mummification and burial goods.

famous.name: Yuya
famous.story_individual:
Yuya was a powerful man in the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. He served as a key adviser for Amenhotep III and carried many titles such as "King’s Lieutenant" and "Master of the Horse."

He married the Egyptian noblewoman Thuya and was the great-grandfather of Tutankhamun through their daughter Tiye, who was the Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III, the ninth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

Because of the many different spelling variants of his name and his physical features, some Egyptologists have speculated that he had foreign origins.

Yuya and his wife were buried in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes.

Zahi Hawass et al. 2010 studied the DNA of 11 royal mummies of the New Kingdom to determine their familial relationships and medical conditions. They studied Yuya and his wife Thuya, their daughter Tiye, and their grandchildren Abhenaten and The Younger Lady (KV35YL) and determined that their grandchildren were the full sibling parents of Tutankhamun.

Gad et al. 2020 further elaborated on the Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family and provided the haplogroup estimates based on DNA-tested Y-STR markers in the mummy remains. Please note that the haplogroup assignment is based on a small number of Y-STR markers as published in the paper. Further DNA testing and analysis may provide updates to the haplogroup assignments.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

Historical information sourced from Wikipedia. Pictured: Mummy mask of Yuya. Photo credit: Jon Bodsworth

famous.name: Tutankhamun
famous.story_individual:
Tutankhamun or King Tut was the last pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. He ruled the New Kingdom from a very young age, becoming a pharaoh at the age of 8 or 9. His reign was short, and he died young at around 18 years old without any heirs, ending the dynasty.

He was buried in the Valley of the Kings and became the most well-recognized symbol of ancient Egypt after his entirely complete and nearly-intact tomb was discovered in 1922. It was the first royal tomb discovered in Egypt that had not been looted by grave robbers. His two infant daughters were also buried in his tomb.

Archaeologist and Egyptologist Howard Carter opens the innermost shrine of King Tutankhamun's tomb (1925)

Zahi Hawass et al. 2010 studied the DNA of 11 royal mummies of the New Kingdom to determine their familial relationships and medical conditions. They studied Tutankhamun and determined that his parents were full siblings and that the unknown mummy KV55 was Tut’s father. They further identified the father as Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV), but this identification has been questioned and said to be uncertain.

Tut’s grandfather, identified as Amenhotep III, shared his paternal lineage, which genealogically traces back to Thutmose I the third pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty. His great-grandparents on his grandmother Tiye’s side were identified as Yuya and Thuya.

Gad et al. 2020 further elaborated on the Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family and provided the haplogroup estimates based on DNA-tested Y-STR markers in the mummy remains. Please note that the haplogroup assignment is based on a small number of Y-STR markers as published in the paper. Further DNA testing and analysis may provide updates to the haplogroup assignments.

Maternal and paternal lineages in King Tutankhamun’s family. Gad et al. 2020 (Figure 2, rearranged for display purposes)

A painted, wooden figure of Tutankhamun found in his royal tomb

Pictured: The funerary mask of Tutankhamun, Roland Unger, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Historical information sourced from Wikipedia.

famous.name: Young Man of Byrsa
famous.story_individual:
Ariche was a young Phoenician man who lived in Carthage, North Africa during the late 6th century BCE. He died between the ages of 19-24 and stood approximately 1.7 meters (5'7") tall. His remains were discovered in 1994 when gardeners at the National Museum of Carthage on Byrsa Hill were planting a tree and uncovered a 4-meter deep burial shaft containing two carved sandstone sarcophagi. The location of his discovery on Byrsa Hill, which was the highest point in ancient Carthage and site of a Phoenician acropolis, led to him being known as the Young Man of Byrsa.

Ariche was given a proper Phoenician burial with significant grave goods, including two Punic amphorae, a lamp, an ivory box containing ointments, food offerings, and several amulets. The care taken in his burial and the quality of the grave goods suggest he was likely from a wealthy or prominent family in Carthage.

Reconstruction of the Young Man of Byrsa based on the skeleton. M. Rais, Public Domain, via Wikipedia Commons.

DNA analysis revealed that through his maternal line, Ariche had European ancestry rather than Near Eastern, African, or Asian. He carried a rare maternal genetic lineage (haplogroup U5b2c1) that was most commonly found in Western Europe, particularly the Iberian Peninsula. This suggests his mother or maternal ancestors likely originated from somewhere in that region, possibly connected to Phoenician maritime trade networks that linked Carthage with southern Spain and Portugal.

His remains are historically significant as they represent the first complete ancient Phoenician genome analyzed. The discovery challenges assumptions about the population makeup of ancient Carthage and provides evidence of the diverse origins of its inhabitants. His case demonstrates the complex interconnections between European and North African populations facilitated by Phoenician maritime trade during the 1st millennium BCE.

Ariche's reconstructed remains and the artifacts from his tomb were part of an international exhibition organized by the National Heritage Institute of Tunis and the Carthage Museum. In 2014, his remains were transferred to the Archaeological Museum of the American University of Beirut for DNA analysis, which helped reveal his unique genetic heritage.

References

  • Matisoo-Smith, E. A., Gosling, A. L., Boocock, J., Kardailsky, O., Kurumilian, Y., Roudesli-Chebbi, S., Badre, L., Morel, P., Sebaï, L. L., & Zalloua, P. A. (2016). A European Mitochondrial Haplotype Identified in Ancient Phoenician Remains from Carthage, North Africa. PLOS ONE, 11(5), e0155046. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0155046

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
